x.A: Geolocation routing sends users by their country or continent, not by closeness, so some users may be sent to a Region that isn't the nearest.
x.B: Geoproximity routing sends users to the closest Region based on geographic distance, and a Network Load Balancer in each Region distributes traffic across the AZs.
x.C: Multivalue answer routing returns several healthy records at random, so users aren't directed to the nearest instances.
x.D: Weighted routing splits traffic by weight regardless of the user's location.

x.A: RDS encryption at rest with KMS managed keys is a single setting, and SSL/TLS certificates secure data in transit between the application and the database, which needs the least operational work.
x.B: IPsec tunnels for encryption in transit need extra infrastructure to set up and manage.
x.C: Third-party application-level encryption adds a lot of development and maintenance, and it isn't needed when RDS encryption is available.
x.D: A VPN for private connectivity adds components to manage and isn't how you normally encrypt connections to RDS.

x.A: RDS automated backups support a maximum retention period of 35 days, so they can't retain data for 90 days.
x.B: Daily manual snapshots and deleting old ones is a manual process that adds operational overhead.
x.C: Aurora cloning is for Aurora databases, and RDS for Oracle doesn't have an Aurora clone feature.
x.D: AWS Backup keeps backups for 90 days through a backup plan, and with continuous backup for RDS, point-in-time restore is available for up to 35 days (including 14 days). It's managed, so it needs the least work.

x.A: Provisioned IOPS storage costs more, and it doesn't scale compute with variable usage.
x.B: Aurora Serverless scales database capacity up and down with actual usage, so for variable, read-heavy usage you pay only for what you use, and it's a managed relational database.
x.C: DynamoDB is not relational, so it doesn't fit a relational database requirement.
x.D: Magnetic storage is slow and read replicas add cost, so it doesn't give the necessary performance cost-effectively.

x.A: A gateway endpoint with an instance profile that lists specific buckets means updating the policy for every new customer bucket, which is a lot of work as buckets are added.
x.B: A NAT gateway sends traffic over the internet to S3, which doesn't restrict access to buckets in the company's account.
x.C: A gateway endpoint keeps traffic on the AWS network, and the instance profile policy denies access to any S3 bucket not owned by the company's account, using a condition key on the resource account. New customer buckets in the account are covered automatically, so it needs the least overhead.
x.D: A NAT gateway uses the internet, and adding Deny bucket policies to every bucket is a lot of work and doesn't limit the instances to the company's buckets.

x.A: IAM roles for each team need a way to be assumed, and managing customized policies per team in the account is more manual work than using IAM Identity Center permission sets.
x.B: IAM Identity Center, which the company already uses, lets you create permission sets with granular access to RDS and S3 and assign them to groups for each team. It's centralized, least-privilege, and needs the least overhead.
x.C: Individual IAM users for every member means long-term credentials and a lot of administration.
x.D: Separate accounts per team with cross-account roles is a heavy structure for access control and adds operational work.

x.A: A bucket policy based on public IP addresses isn't secure, because IP addresses can be shared or spoofed, and the data center's address range isn't an identity.
x.B: IAM Roles Anywhere lets workloads outside AWS get temporary security credentials by using X.509 certificates, so the application can assume a role with access to the bucket without long-term keys.
x.C: Access keys from an IAM user are long-term credentials stored on the virtual machine, which is insecure.
x.D: Storing IAM user keys in Secrets Manager is still using long-term credentials, and the application needs credentials to read them.

x.A: A Direct Connect connection for each new account is expensive and slow to provision.
x.B: VPC endpoints are for accessing AWS services privately, not for routing to on-premises directory and DNS services.
x.C: A VPN connection from each account to the Direct Connect VPC is a lot of connections to build and manage, and VPN has less consistent performance.
x.D: A transit gateway with the Direct Connect attached acts as a central hub, so new accounts' VPCs just attach to it to reach the on-premises network services consistently and cost-effectively.

x.A: CloudFront with the ALB as the origin caches content and accelerates dynamic content over the AWS global network, so it improves global performance cost-effectively.
x.B: Route 53 geographic routing chooses the endpoint, but the application is only in one Region, so it doesn't improve performance for distant users.
x.C: A website in S3 can only serve static content, so it can't serve dynamic content, and public read access is insecure.
x.D: Direct Connect connects networks to AWS and isn't a way to serve millions of customers around the world.

x.A: S3 Standard has the highest storage price, even for data that isn't used for months.
x.B: S3 Intelligent-Tiering moves data between access tiers automatically as use changes, with no retrieval fees, and keeps the highest durability across multiple AZs with high availability. It's cost-effective for varying access patterns.
x.C: Deep Archive has retrieval delays, so it isn't suitable for data used continuously during business hours.
x.D: One Zone-IA stores data in a single AZ, so it doesn't maintain the highest level of durability and availability.

x.A: A single NFS server on EC2 with one EBS volume is a single point of failure and isn't highly available.
x.B: FSx for Windows File Server in a single AZ isn't highly available, and SMB for a Linux application means code changes.
x.C: One instance with two volumes is still a single instance and can't be shared among multiple instances.
x.D: EFS is a managed, highly available, shared file system with NFS that all instances can mount at once, so the application needs almost no code changes.

x.A: A Network Load Balancer handles TCP traffic across the instances in both AZs at a low cost with high performance.
x.B: An Auto Scaling group automatically adds and removes instances as the number of users changes, so the application scales.
x.C: An ALB works with HTTP and HTTPS, so it doesn't fit TCP communication, and costs more.
x.D: Manually adding instances isn't automatic scaling.
x.E: A Gateway Load Balancer is for virtual appliances, not for distributing user traffic to the application.

x.A: An Organizations tag policy defines the tag key and allowed values (sensitive and nonsensitive), and enforcement makes tagging with other values noncompliant on the EC2 instances. Attached to the OU, it standardizes the tags.
x.B: An SCP can't define tag values and enforce them in this way. Tag policies do that.
x.C: Tag policies can't deny running instances without a tag or prevent deleting tags. They only standardize tag keys and values.
x.D: SCPs can deny creating instances when the tag isn't specified and deny deleting tags, so identities can't create untagged instances or remove the tag.
x.E: A Config rule with a Lambda function to delete noncompliant resources acts after creation, and doesn't prevent untagged creation or tag deletion.

x.A: Setting a 30 day retention for automated backups doesn't use AWS Backup, and AWS Backup doesn't remove manual backups either, so it's extra and costs more.
x.B: Disabling automated backups deletes the existing automated backups, which the company wants to keep for 30 days.
x.C: Setting the automated backup retention to 30 days keeps automated backups for 30 days, and manual snapshots stay until deleted, so deleting the ones older than 30 days meets the policy at no extra cost.
x.D: Disabling automated backups removes the existing automated backups, and using CloudFormation to delete snapshots is more work.

x.A: DataSync is a data transfer service, not storage that an application uses over NFS.
x.B: EBS is block storage and doesn't provide NFS access, and the application can't be changed.
x.C: EFS is a managed NFS file system, so the application keeps using NFS with no changes, and it's highly available and scalable.
x.D: EMRFS is for EMR clusters to access S3, not an NFS file system.

x.A: Scanning S3 for new data means the application polls, and a flood of data could still overwhelm it, with no ordered buffering.
x.B: API Gateway and Lambda processing each item concurrently could be throttled or overwhelm downstream systems, and data could be lost if processing fails.
x.C: An SQS queue stores incoming data durably, so no data is lost if the application is overwhelmed. The application polls and processes messages at its own pace, and failed messages can be retried. It has the least operational overhead.
x.D: A DynamoDB table with polling and TTL needs more design and capacity management, and querying for new data isn't a natural queue.

x.A: A public subnet RDS cluster exposes the database to the internet, which isn't the most secure.
x.B: RDS in private subnets with a Site-to-Site VPN from the office gives direct connectivity to the client over an encrypted tunnel, without exposing the database to the internet.
x.C: Security groups can't allow on-premises IP ranges to reach a private subnet over the internet. The database has no route to the internet in private subnets.
x.D: A public subnet RDS exposes the database to the internet, and cluster users aren't a network control.

x.A: An Auto Scaling group doesn't affect data transfer charges between instances.
x.B: Data transfer within a Region between AZs is still charged, so being in the same Region isn't enough.
x.C: Data transferred between EC2 instances in the same Availability Zone using private IP addresses is free, so placing all the instances in one AZ reduces data transfer costs.
x.D: Instances in multiple AZs pay cross-AZ transfer charges, which increases cost.

x.A: Secrets Manager stores credentials encrypted with a KMS key and supports built-in rotation for Aurora with a custom schedule of 14 days. It needs the least operational effort.
x.B: Parameter Store has no native rotation, so you'd build a Lambda function.
x.C: A credentials file on EFS with a custom Lambda rotation takes a lot of custom work.
x.D: A credentials file in S3 with a custom Lambda rotation also needs custom work, and the application has to keep downloading the file.

x.A: Lambda has a 15 minute limit, so it can't process videos that take up to 20 minutes.
x.B: ECS on Fargate runs containers without servers for as long as the processing takes, scales with demand, and S3 Intelligent-Tiering stores the video content cost-effectively. It's scalable and cost-effective.
x.C: EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group work, but you manage the servers and pay for idle capacity, so it's less cost-effective.
x.D: EKS on EC2 is more to manage, RDS in a single AZ isn't resilient, and Glacier Deep Archive isn't suited to videos users consume daily.

x.A: Self-managed nodes mean managing the underlying compute, which the company wants to avoid.
x.B: Managed node groups automate some node management, but you still manage EC2 instances, so it isn't the least overhead.
x.C: Fargate runs the pods without nodes to provision or manage, and a Fargate profile selects which pods run on it. It has the least operational overhead.
x.D: Karpenter with managed node groups still provisions and manages EC2 nodes, even if it automates scaling.

x.A: A self-managed database on EC2 Spot Instances can be interrupted, and you manage the database yourself.
x.B: RDS doesn't have an on-demand capacity mode, since that's a DynamoDB option, and RDS doesn't scale automatically with traffic.
x.C: Aurora Serverless is a structured (relational) database that scales capacity with application traffic, is managed, and takes automated backups to S3. You pay only for the capacity used, so it's the most cost-effective.
x.D: A self-managed NoSQL database isn't a structured relational database, and Glacier isn't a place for automated database backups you may need quickly.

x.A: A gateway VPC endpoint for S3 sends traffic to S3 over the AWS network instead of the public endpoint, with a route in the subnet route table. It has no extra cost.
x.B: S3 buckets can't be moved inside a VPC, because S3 is a Regional service outside the VPC.
x.C: An access point still uses S3's public endpoints unless it's reached through an endpoint, so it doesn't change the network path by itself.
x.D: Direct Connect connects on-premises networks to AWS and isn't used between a VPC and S3.

x.A: Redshift is a data warehouse, not a store for the product catalog used by a transactional website, and it's costly.
x.B: ElastiCache for Redis caches the product catalog in memory, and lazy loading fills the cache as items are requested. Since the catalog changes infrequently, most searches are served from the cache, reducing database CPU.
x.C: Adding web servers doesn't reduce the load on the database, which is the bottleneck.
x.D: Multi-AZ improves availability, not performance, and throttling queries would make searches slower.

x.A: S3 File Gateway provides file shares, but the on-premises data is on block storage, so applications that use block storage would need to change.
x.B: A Volume Gateway with cached volumes stores the full data set in S3 and keeps the frequently accessed data in a local cache, so applications get low latency for hot data, and the 5 TB isn't limited by on-premises space. iSCSI matches block storage.
x.C: Stored volumes keep the entire data set on premises, so the limited space problem isn't solved.
x.D: A Tape Gateway is for backup applications with virtual tapes, not for primary block storage that applications read with low latency.
